India finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with 39 medals to its name - 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze. It placed India in fourth place behind Australia, England and Canada. Boxing and athletics produced the most medals (10) with weightlifting (8) and para-athletics (6) next in the order.In the truncated quadrennial event, held without shooting, wrestling, badminton, table tennis and field hockey, all of which have contributed significantly to India's coffers in the past, the country finished with 22 medals fewer than the 2022 edition in Birmingham (61 medals).Gulveer Singh emerged as the only multiple medallist for India at the Games. His silver in 10,000m and bronze in 5,000m made him the first Indian track and field athlete to win two individual medals at a single CWG edition.The Aligarh-born Naib Subedar made his international breakthrough with a bronze medal in the 5000m at the 2023 Asian Athletics Championships and followed it up with another third-place finish at the rescheduled 2022 Asian Games.The 28-year-old national record holder in 5000m, 10,000m, one mile and half-marathon trains regularly at the high-performance centre in Colorado Springs, USA, where steps towards his multiple feats and medals are forged.A Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) athlete, he's been assisted with Rs 30.40 lakh during this CWG cycle and Rs 25.32 lakh under the Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC).Behind every medal is days and weeks of training and preparation backed by government and funding by private players.Before the Glasgow Games got underway, the track and field athletes and para-athletes underwent training at the Spala Olympic Training Centre in Poland; boxers spent time in Belfast; the lifters travelled to Birmingham while the Artistic Gymnastics team set camp in South Essex.All such tours were sponsored by the government through its ACTC fund and TOPS.TOPS, a division formed in September 2014, operates as the Sports Ministry's flagship programme to support India's athletes win medals at the Olympics. It is presently headed by Col. Nachhatar Singh Johal, who represented the country in sailing at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.Earlier this year, TOPS' ambit increased to 27 sports with six getting priority: archery, badminton, boxing, hockey, shooting and wrestling.Subsequently, Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), which was created last year to provide support to select athletes was disbanded this year. It had begun with an initial pool of 16 disciplines and 37 athletes.However, its responsibilities will now be shared between TOPS and Training of Elite Athletes and Management Support (TEAMS) divisions. TOPS and TEAMS will manage day-to-day operations, development, and coordination for 27 specific disciplines.TOPS selects athletes based on their medal potential rather than a single qualifying criterion. The scheme assesses recent international performances, world rankings, consistency at the elite level, long-term progression and potential to win medals at the Olympics and other major events. Recommendations from the Mission Olympic Cell (MOC), National Sports Federations (NSFs), coaches, foreign experts and sports science teams also play a key role.Athletes are divided into two categories:Core Group: Established athletes with immediate medal prospects.Development Group: Emerging athletes being prepared for future Olympic cycles.Their performances are monitored regularly to ensure support matches their progress.There is no fixed annual funding cap under TOPS. Instead, assistance is tailored to each athlete's requirements, depending on their sport, training programme and competition calendar.Funding can cover:For athletes in high-performance Olympic and Paralympic disciplines requiring overseas training and advanced support systems, annual funding can run into several lakhs or even crores of rupees. Every proposal undergoes technical and financial scrutiny before approval by the MOC.TOPS follows a two-pronged approach—backing athletes capable of winning medals immediately while simultaneously investing in future prospects.This is achieved through:The objective is to maximise India's medal chances today while creating a pipeline of athletes for future Olympic, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games and Paralympic cycles.Athletes are monitored continuously, with periodic reviews conducted by the Mission Olympic Cell alongside NSFs, coaches and technical experts.Reviews consider:TOPS follows a performance-linked funding model. If an athlete consistently underperforms, remains inactive without valid reasons or repeatedly misses agreed benchmarks, financial support can be reduced or withdrawn after evaluation.However, genuine circumstances such as injuries, rehabilitation or long-term planning are also taken into account before any decision is made.Yes. TOPS has expanded beyond traditional funding to provide a comprehensive high-performance support system.Support can include:The aim is to give Indian athletes access to the same integrated support systems available in leading sporting nations, with greater emphasis on recovery, injury management, mental resilience and scientific preparation.TOPS says its funding decisions are guided by transparency, accountability and merit. Every proposal passes through multiple stages of evaluation involving NSFs, coaches, sports science experts, the MOC and financial scrutiny under government procedures.Funding decisions are based on measurable criteria, including:The scheme also incorporates periodic reviews, stakeholder consultations, documented approval processes and audit mechanisms to ensure public funds are used effectively. Its stated vision is that no Indian athlete with genuine medal potential should miss out on world-class preparation because of financial constraints.It is now 10 years to the 2036 Olympics, a Summer Games that India intends to host in Ahmedabad. If awarded, the goal there will not just be showcase its culture and ability to host an event of such scale but to compete with the best. To that end, the Union Cabinet has approved a revamped Khelo India Scheme and enhanced assistance to National Sports Federations (NSFs).For the period of 2026-27 to 2030-31, which covers the 2030 CWG, LA 2028, Brisbane 2032 and five years leading to the 2036 Summer Games, a combined outlay of Rs 36,441 crore has been planned - Rs 29,054 crore towards Khelo India Scheme and Rs 7,387 crore to the NSFs.The revamped, and enhanced, Khelo India Scheme is nearly eight times the previous budget allocation (Rs 2532.22 crore from 2021-2026) towards grassroots development.After the positive returns at the Commonwealth Games, a tougher test awaits the Indian contingent later in the year at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan from September 19. And then further down the line at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, the necessary off-the-field steps for which have already been taken.
Article Summary: Neeraj Chopra won the silver medal in the men's javelin throw final at the Commonwealth Games 2026, in Glasgow, Scotland. Chopra will compete for India at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. He will be competing for India in the 4x100m and 4x400m relay events.

Article Title: 'A coterie hijacked him': Report claims Pakistan federation distanced itself from Arshad Nadeem before CWG flop
Article Text:
Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem (PTI Photo)

Federation 'distanced itself' from Olympic champion's preparations

Coach admits Nadeem was underprepared

Pakistan sporting structure under scrutiny

'A coterie hijacked him': Mentors question Nadeem's preparation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem has found himself at the centre of growing criticism following his disappointing Commonwealth Games campaign in Glasgow, with questions now being raised not just about his form but also about the support system that surrounded him in the lead-up to the competition.The defending Commonwealth Games champion endured one of the worst outings of his career, finishing ninth after failing to produce a throw beyond 80 metres. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage clinched the gold medal, while India's Neeraj Chopra and Yashvir Singh completed a historic South Asian podium with silver and bronze respectively.But as scrutiny intensified over Nadeem's performance, reports from Pakistan suggested the Olympic champion had effectively been left to prepare on his own after the Pakistan Amateur Athletics Federation (PAAF) allegedly distanced itself from his training programme following a dispute over the retention of his long-time coach Salman Butt According to a PTI report, the PAAF largely withdrew support from the star javelin thrower after disagreements emerged last year over his coaching setup. The report claimed that several requests made by Nadeem regarding his training programme were not entertained, while the Pakistan Sports Board also did not release funds to facilitate foreign coaches or trainers.Instead of training overseas under renowned South African coach Terseus Liebenberg, who had guided him before his Olympic triumph, Nadeem spent his Commonwealth Games build-up in Lahore with Salman Butt and local trainers.The contrast with India's preparation was striking. While Neeraj Chopra completed his final rehabilitation and training block in Biel, Switzerland, fellow Indian javelin throwers Yashvir Singh and Rohit Yadav trained in Spala, Poland, alongside foreign coaches and support staff before heading to Glasgow.The differing approaches were reflected in the final standings as India secured two medals, while Nadeem failed to qualify among the top eight after the opening three rounds.Nadeem had arrived in Glasgow with limited competitive exposure, having competed in only one preparatory meet in Switzerland during 2026. He also trained almost exclusively in Lahore despite the vastly different weather conditions between Pakistan and Scotland.His long-time coach Salman Butt admitted the Olympic champion was far from his best and acknowledged he was underprepared for the Games.Former Pakistan Athletics Federation president Akram Sahi also blamed negligence and inadequate preparation for the dramatic decline."Since Nadeem's Olympic gold medal a coterie has hijacked him and never let him come to me," Sahi told Telecom Asia Sport."This result in Glasgow is hugely disappointing... the signs were imminent for the last several months as there was negligence and lack of training."Another mentor, speaking anonymously, argued that Nadeem had become complacent and failed to invest sufficiently in elite overseas training after receiving substantial financial rewards following his Olympic success.Nadeem's disappointing campaign has reignited debate over Pakistan's sporting ecosystem.Former Olympic boxing bronze medallist Hussain Shah described the situation as a reflection of systemic shortcomings."This is an athlete who is self-made and comes from a village and belongs to a low-income family. But he brought so much glory to Pakistan with his gold medals. And yet he couldn't prepare properly for the CWG. It is a sad reflection on our sports structure," Shah said.Pakistan's campaign in Glasgow also exposed wider concerns. Boxer Fatima Zehra, who secured the country's only medal with bronze, also lamented the lack of quality preparation and international exposure, saying better training could have helped her challenge for gold.The criticism did not stop with Pakistan's athletics authorities. Two of Nadeem's former mentors also questioned the Olympic champion's preparation, alleging that a lack of quality training and poor decisions contributed to his disappointing campaign.Akram Sahi, the former Pakistan Athletics Federation president who helped identify Nadeem's talent in 2018, claimed the warning signs had been visible for months."Since Nadeem's Olympic gold medal a coterie has hijacked him and never let him come to me," Sahi told Telecom Asia Sport."This result in Glasgow is hugely disappointing for someone who has risen to new heights, but the signs were imminent for the last several months as there was negligence and lack of training."Another mentor, speaking anonymously, echoed those concerns, suggesting Nadeem had not trained adequately after returning from Haj and had become overly dependent on official support."He won the Olympics after he got extensive training from his South African coach Terseus Liebenberg. His training stints at Northwest University Potchefstroom also helped him clinch Olympic gold. Now he waited for the federation and government to send him to South Africa for training.He should have invested in himself rather than waiting for someone else," the mentor said.The mentor also questioned Nadeem's current coaching setup, claiming his long-time coach Salman Butt lacked specialist expertise in javelin and that the Olympic champion had become distracted by business ventures after receiving substantial financial rewards following his Paris triumph.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem finished ninth in the javelin throw at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Reports suggest the Pakistan Amateur Athletics Federation (PAAF) 'distanced itself' from his training programme following a dispute over the retention of his long-time coach Salman Butt. Former Pakistan Athletics Federation president Akram Sahi blamed negligence and inadequate preparation for the dramatic decline. Former Olympic boxing bronze medallist Hussain Shah described the situation as a reflection of systemic shortcomings.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Relay flop raises Asian Games alarm
Article Text:
Vishal TK (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Even as India celebrated a strong athletics campaign at the Commonwealth Games — highlighted by three para athletics gold medals to go with five silver and five bronze from the able-bodied contingent — attention has now shifted to the disappointing performance of the mixed 4x400m relay team.The quartet, which made the cut after surviving a rigorous selection process that saw the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) reject all the other relay combinations, failed to deliver on the biggest stage.Vishal TK, who set a national record this season with a personal best of 44.98 seconds in May, clocked a below-par 46.1 in the opening lap in the final. Ansa Babu then struggled to match the quality of the field, clocking 54.1 while rivals, led by Jamaica’s Leah Anderson (50.8 seconds), comfortably ran under 52 seconds.Santosh Kumar Tamilarasan (46.4 seconds) and Rashdeep Kaur (53.72 seconds) were unable to change the complexion of the race as India finished sixth and last in the final rankings after Australia was disqualified and Zambia failed to finish.“It seems India’s top runners peaked too early this season. Rajesh ran 45.26 in March but his performance dipped in Glasgow. Rajesh is one of our key relay runners and, with Mohammed Anas and Amoj Jacob still recovering from injuries, he is now the most experienced member of the squad.It will take a miracle for our relay runners to improve enough before the Asian Games next month,” another coach said.Rajesh, who clocked 47.00 seconds in the heats, was replaced by Santosh for the final. Several coaches who monitored the team’s preparations also questioned whether the expertise of foreign coach Jason Alexander Dawson was being fully utilised.“Two coaches training two separate groups of athletes simply doesn’t work. Whoever can’t cope with Jason’s workload shifts to the Indian coach. Ideally, all the 400m runners should train under one programme and one brain,” one coach said, referring to the parallel coaching setup under Dawson and Raj Mohan in Thiruvananthapuram.A former national coach, who had previously handled the relay squad, urged patience. “You can’t call Vishal a sub-45 runner unless he consistently runs below 45 seconds. I’m optimistic our relay squads will bounce back and perform well at the Asian Games. Earlier, India was stronger in the women’s 4x400m relay, but now the men’s team has become more competitive,” he said.Meanwhile, AFI has reportedly decided not to field the men’s 4x100m relay team at the Asian Games while clearing the remaining relay squads.
Article Summary: The mixed 4x400m relay team failed to deliver on the biggest stage. Vishal TK, who set a national record this season with a personal best of 44.98 seconds in May, clocked a below-par 46.1 in the opening lap in the final. Ansa Babu then struggled to match the quality of the field, clocking 54.1.

Article Title: Glasgow done, all eyes on 'Amdavad 2030': India's campaign offers both promise and warning signs
Article Text:
Indian boxer Jaismine Lamboria and other athletes during the closing ceremony of the CWG 2026. (PTI Photo)

Athletics leads the way



Boxers make a statement



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Judokas earn their place in the spotlight



PUNE: The Glasgow Commonwealth Games are over. The baton passes to India for the Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, dubbed ‘Amdavad 2030’. With the event returning home after 20 years, India will be aiming not only to stage a better Games than Delhi 2010 but also to improve on its best-ever medal haul. At the 2010 Delhi Games, India won a record 101 medals to finish second in the overall standings.For Indian sport, Glasgow offered a mixed picture. The 39 medals collected this time were fewer than the 61 in Birmingham 2022, 66 in Gold Coast 2018 and 64 in Glasgow 2014. More importantly, those medals came from just six sports. By contrast, India’s medals had come from 17 sports in 2010, 11 in 2014, 15 in 2018 and 13 in 2022.The explanation lies partly in the programme itself. Glasgow did not include sports where India has traditionally been strong. India has won 135 medals in shooting between 1966 and 2018, excluding the 1970 Edinburgh edition. Wrestling has fetched India 114 medals across 18 editions since 1934. Yet Glasgow had no shooting, wrestling, hockey, badminton, archery or table tennis, which together had contributed 67 medals for India in Delhi 2010.As India prepares to host in 2030, the focus will be on retaining the positives from Glasgow while also bringing back its strongest disciplines.Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000m long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para-athletics adding up to 16 medals. What stood out most was the history made by Gulveer Singh, who won silver in the 10,000m and bronze in the 5,000m and Tejaswin Shankar, who claimed decathlon bronze.Yash Vir Singh also broke new ground by winning a javelin bronze in a field featuring Olympic and world champions, as well as world leaders and record holders. The para-athletes contributed three gold, two silver and one bronze, even as the 4x400m relay team had to settle for sixth place.“The performance was way better than expected. This has been a good result and it will only improve in the years to come. The result reflects the policies that the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) has adopted in the past few years,” former World Championships bronze medallist and current AFI senior vice-president Anju Bobby George told TOI.“Now we plan the training programme according to individual athletes’ requirements rather than designing a blanket programme for everyone. Some athletes train in the USA, some in Europe, because that is what best suits their future. The results are definitely going to improve in 2030 and beyond, as we also plan to host the Olympics,” she added.Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. While the level of competition at the Commonwealth Games is not as demanding as at the Asian Games or Olympics, the performances will still provide a valuable confidence boost.“It is not as if these were the only medals our boxers have won so far. We had world champions, an Olympic medallist and Asian Games and Asian Championships winners at the Glasgow CWG. The field may not have been as strong as the Asiad, but it was not weak either.A good show at a competition like this gives a boost to the boxers,” 2008 Beijing Olympics bronze medallist Vijender Singh told TOI.With two historic gold and three medals overall, Indian judokas Asmita Dey, Harsh Singh and Yamini Mourya also deserve special mention. A sport that has often struggled for attention in the past appears to be finding its footing.If judo can continue on this trajectory, the possibilities are immense. With 15 medal events at the Olympics and proper investment and a cleaner administrative setup, India has genuine medal potential at the world level too.
Article Summary: Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000M long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para- athletics adding up to 16 medals. Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. Judo also deserves special mention, with two historic gold and three medals overall.

Article Title: Forging champions in Olive Green: How the Army Sports Institute has become India’s premier high performance centre
Article Text:
Ankush Panghal, Jaismine Lamboria, Arundhati Choudhary and Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (Image credit: Agencies)

Building Champions, Not Just Athletes

Boxing: The Crown Jewel

The High Performance Advantage

Beyond Boxing

A Model for India’s Olympic Ambitions

NEW DELHI: The resounding success of Indian Army athletes at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow is far more than a medal-winning campaign—it is the culmination of years of scientific planning, relentless discipline and institutional excellence. At the heart of this success stands the Army Sports Institute (ASI), Pune, India’s premier military high performance centre, which has once again demonstrated why it is regarded as one of the country’s finest centres for elite athlete development.With Army boxers contributing an extraordinary haul of 8 medals at the CWG, ASI’s contribution to Indian boxing has reached unprecedented heights. From Olympic hopefuls to Commonwealth champions, the institute continues to produce athletes capable of competing—and winning—against the very best in the world.Established in 2005, the Army Sports Institute was envisioned as the Indian Army ’s flagship project to identify, nurture and develop sporting excellence. Twenty-five years later, that vision has evolved into one of the country’s most successful high-performance ecosystems.Unlike conventional training centres, ASI integrates every aspect of athlete development under one roof. Elite coaching, sports science, strength and conditioning, biomechanics, nutrition, psychology, physiotherapy, recovery management and performance analytics operate seamlessly to maximise every athlete’s potential.This holistic approach has transformed ASI into a benchmark for high-performance sport in India.Boxing has emerged as one of ASI’s greatest success stories.The institute’s talent identification programme scouts promising youngsters from across India and systematically develops them through the Boys and Girls Sports Companies before transitioning the best performers into elite national-level competitors.The results are unmistakable.At Glasgow 2026, Army boxers dominated the competition, winning medals across multiple weight categories and forming the backbone of India’s historic boxing campaign. Their performances reflected exceptional technical preparation, tactical maturity and the mental resilience that are hallmarks of Army training. India’s boxing team produced its best-ever CWG performance with seven gold and three silver medals overall, underscoring the depth of the programme.Success at ASI is not accidental.Every training session is data-driven. Athlete workloads are scientifically monitored. Recovery protocols minimise injury risk. Nutrition plans are customised. Performance is analysed through modern sports science and technology.This integrated approach ensures that athletes peak when it matters most—at international championships.Equally important is the military ethos that defines every athlete trained at ASI: discipline, resilience, teamwork and the determination to perform under pressure.While boxing has become a flagship discipline, ASI’s excellence extends across athletics, wrestling, weightlifting, diving, fencing, archery and several Olympic sports.While boxing led the Army Sports Institute’s remarkable CWG campaign, its excellence extended well beyond the ring. Army athletes scripted history in athletics with a series of landmark performances. Naib Subedar Gulveer Singh became the first Indian ever to win a silver medal in the men’s 10,000m and followed it with a historic bronze in the 5,000m—the first medal by an Indian in the event at the Commonwealth Games. In doing so, he also became the first Indian track and field athlete to win two medals at a single CWG.Adding to the historic achievements, Naib Subedar Sarvesh Kushare won the silver medal in High Jump, marking India’s first-ever CWG medal in the men’s high jump. In the weightlifting arena Hav Ajaya Babu won a silver medal and created a new record in Snatch category. Together, these breakthrough performances reaffirm that the Army Sports Institute is not merely producing champions in one discipline but is emerging as India’s most successful multi-sport high-performance centre, consistently delivering athletes capable of rewriting the nation’s sporting history.The institute has consistently produced Olympians, Asian Games medallists, CWG champions and national record holders. Many of India’s finest sporting achievements over the past decade have carried the unmistakable imprint of the Army Sports Institute.As India intensifies its preparations for future Olympic Games, the Army Sports Institute provides a proven blueprint for sustained international success.Its combination of early talent identification, world-class coaching, cutting-edge sports science and unwavering institutional support has created a system capable of producing champions year after year.The Glasgow CWG have once again reaffirmed an enduring truth: when India celebrates sporting excellence, the Army Sports Institute is often at the heart of that success.From nurturing young talent to producing Commonwealth champions, ASI continues to live its motto—transforming potential into podium finishes and inspiring a new generation of athletes to wear the Tricolour with pride.The remarkable contribution of Army athletes at Glasgow is not merely a medal tally; it is a testament to twenty-five years of vision, investment and unwavering commitment to sporting excellence. Champions are not born overnight—they are forged in Olive Green.
Article Summary: Army Sports Institute, Pune, is India’s premier military high performance centre. Boxers dominated the competition at Glasgow 2026, winning medals across multiple weight categories. Army athletes scripted history in athletics with a series of landmark performances. Naib Subedar Gulveer Singh became the first Indian ever to win a silver medal in the 10,000m.

Article Title: CWG para champions complain against IOA staff, seek action over alleged 'misconduct, disrespectful behaviour'
Article Text:
Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi. (PTI Photo)

NEW DELHI: Fresh from scripting history at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, India’s men’s T47 100m gold and silver medallists Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi have lodged formal complaints with the sports ministry and the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) against an IOA media committee member, alleging rude and disrespectful behaviour towards the country’s para athletes.The complaints have been filed separately by Gavit, Basil and para athletics coach Pushpa NP, who was part of the Indian contingent in Glasgow. It is learnt that Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) CEO Rahul Swami has also submitted a similar complaint to the ministry and the IOA.According to sources, the complaints name Sarvesh Kedia, an IOA media committee member who travelled to Glasgow as one of the Indian contingent’s press attaches and was attached to the chef-de-mission’s office. Kedia was among the 14 IOA officials accompanying India’s combined able-bodied and para athletes’ contingent.In a complaint accessed by TOI, Pushpa alleged that Kedia “was talking loudly with our medal winners Dilip Gavit and Basil and coaches” and said the incident involved him and chief para athletics coach Satyanarayana. She urged the authorities to ensure that Kedia “is not involved in any para athletics media interaction” in future and sought appropriate action against him.The alleged incident took place on July 30 after Gavit clocked 10.71 seconds — a Games record — to become India’s first male para athlete to win a Commonwealth Games athletics gold medal. Basil followed with a season-best of 10.83 seconds to claim silver as India completed a historic 1-2 finish in the men’s T47 100m final.According to sources, a heated argument broke out between Kedia and Satyanarayana over facilitating the athletes’ media interactions before they proceeded for mandatory dope-control procedures. The exchange allegedly escalated into a brief physical altercation before coaches and athletes stepped in to defuse the situation.The incident reportedly left several members of the para athletics contingent deeply upset, prompting the athletes, coaches and PCI officials to submit formal complaints to the sports ministry and the IOA seeking action.
Article Summary: Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi have lodged formal complaints with the sports ministry and the Indian Olympic Association. They allege rude and disrespectful behaviour towards the country’s para athletes. The complaints name Sarvesh Kedia, an IOA media committee member.

Article Title: Shoulder surgery, 7 months out, one unforgettable throw: How Yash Vir Singh won CWG bronze
Article Text:
Yash Vir Singh

Before Glasgow glory came years of struggle

Yash Vir Singh (Special Arrangements)

The father who never gave up on Yash Vir

Yash Vir Singh with his father (Special Arrangements)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Before Yash Vir Singh walked up for his sixth and final throw in the men's javelin final at Scotstoun Stadium, two voices stayed with him.One came from Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra."You're throwing well. Just keep it straight and believe in yourself. It's your last throw, just make sure you don't foul. You can do it."The other came from his father and coach, Rai Singh."It's the last throw. Put everything into it."Seconds later, the javelin landed at 85.41 metres.Yash Vir leapt from seventh place to the bronze medal position, registering a personal best by almost three metres. The effort not only earned him a place on the podium alongside Neeraj Chopra, who took silver behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga, but also made him only the third Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in men's javelin. For the first time in the history of the event, two Indians shared the Commonwealth Games podium.The medal came in one of the strongest men's javelin fields assembled at a Commonwealth Games.The Glasgow final featured one of the strongest javelin fields assembled at a Commonwealth Games. Besides Neeraj and Yash Vir, India also had Rohit Yadav in the final. Reigning Commonwealth Games champion Arshad Nadeem was back to defend his title.Former world champion Anderson Peters of Grenada, Trinidad and Tobago's Keshorn Walcott and former Commonwealth champion Julius Yego were all in the fray. Rumesh Tharanga, meanwhile, arrived in Glasgow after a series of impressive performances and eventually walked away with gold.For much of the evening, Yash Vir remained in the background.Having squeezed into the final in 10th place during qualification, few would have backed the Indian Railways ticket collector to leave Glasgow with a medal. His best throw heading into the final round measured 81.33m, leaving him seventh in the standings with one attempt remaining.Then came his final attempt."I'd made up my mind - today it was do or die. I shouted it out and then went for the throw. It wasn't easy. I'd already committed two fouls and even my fifth throw was only 76.95 metres. My only thought was to produce my personal best. I had nothing to lose. But there was a hunger built up over the last four years. I'll always remember that 85.41m throw. I'm immensely grateful to God," Yash Vir told TimesofIndia.com.The conditions hardly made life easier. Several leading throwers struggled to find consistency as gusty conditions made it difficult to judge the release. Yash Vir adjusted quickly."I quickly calculated the wind conditions. Then I increased my speed a bit and made a slight change to my technique according to the wind pressure. The plan was simple - release the javelin with full power. That's it. The plan worked. I'm happy that I finally crossed the 85-metre mark. My previous best was over 83 metres at the Inter State Championships."The bronze medal was the culmination of four years spent fighting through injury, surgery and rehabilitation, all while holding on to a promise he had made to himself."Main wapsi karke dikhaunga.[I'll make a comeback]."The promise was made in 2022.During a training session, Yash Vir injured his shoulder. The damage was serious. One of the muscles in his rotator cuff - the supraspinatus - had been affected, leaving him in constant pain and eventually requiring surgery at the Abhinav Bindra Targeting Performance (ABTP) Centre in Jaipur.The operation was successful, but it came with another challenge. Doctors ruled him out of competition for at least seven months. For an athlete whose life revolved around throwing the javelin, the rehabilitation was as much a mental battle as a physical one."It was an extremely difficult time. All I wanted was to return to the field," Yash Vir said."The surgery went well and my treatment was completed successfully. Dr Harshvardhan Singh and Dr Aditi Thakur are like God to me. They gave me the confidence that I would be able to throw the javelin again the way I always had. Today, I am here because of them. I owe them a lot."Unable to train, he spent months confined to bed. There was little he could do physically, so he tried to stay connected with the sport in every way possible. He watched videos of his old competitions, relived some of his best throws and immersed himself in motivational books, refusing to let the dream of competing again fade away.When he eventually returned in 2023, the signs were encouraging. His comeback competition ended with a silver medal. Strong performances followed over the next two seasons, eventually earning him a place in India's squad for the Commonwealth Games.Yet, despite steady progress, Yash Vir travelled to Glasgow with little fanfare.The spotlight naturally remained on Chopra, India's Olympic and world champion, while Rohit Yadav completed the three-member Indian contingent. Yash Vir entered the competition as an outsider, having qualified for the final in 10th place.Throughout the journey, one person remained at the centre of it all - his father, Rai Singh."Now, I don't want to look back. A Commonwealth Games medal means a lot to me. You can say this is just the beginning," he said.Behind that journey has been one constant figure. His father. Rai Singh is much more than Yash Vir's coach.A former national-level javelin thrower himself, Rai won multiple national medals and Railway championship titles before becoming an athletics coach with the Indian Railways. An NIS Diploma holder, he has guided his son's career from the very beginning, overseeing not just his technique but every aspect of his routine.Long before international medals entered the conversation, father and son spent countless hours training at the Railway Ground near Jaipur railway station.The first javelin wasn't even made of metal. It was bamboo."My father is very strict. He believes in discipline. He takes care of my training, schedule, diet and every single aspect of my life. I may be his son, but he is even stricter with me than anyone else," Yash Vir said."Whatever I am today is because of him. Foreign coaches come and go after a while, but it is my father who has taught me everything from the very beginning."Even now, the technical discussions happen at home."I don't know much about biomechanics. My father understands it really well. Whatever plan he gives me, whether it's about intensity, power, run-up or the release angle, everything comes from him."At Scotstoun Stadium, Rai Singh watched from above the runway, shouting instructions after every attempt. He had never received the opportunity to compete on one of athletics' biggest stages himself.On Saturday evening in Glasgow, he watched his son stand on the Commonwealth Games podium with a bronze medal around his neck. For Yash Vir, the medal represented a personal best, a national milestone and the fulfilment of a promise he had made to himself four years ago.
Article Summary: Yash Vir Singh wins bronze in the men's javelin at the Commonwealth Games. He is the third Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in the event. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga won gold and India's Neeraj Chopra took silver.

Article Title: Coincidence... or a sign? Vinicius Jr wipes entire Instagram amid Real Madrid contract talks and Arsenal interest
Article Text:
Vinicius Jr deletes everything from Instagram as Real Madrid future remains under the spotlight/ Image: AP

Entire Instagram profile cleared

Return to training brought encouraging signs

Real Madrid TV

Transfer speculation has continued

Contract remains the central issue

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Vinicius Jr has removed every post, photograph and highlight from his Instagram account, while also deleting his biography and profile picture, in the latest development surrounding his uncertain Real Madrid future. The Brazilian returned to pre-season training under José Mourinho earlier this week and has publicly spoken positively about life under the new coach, but his unexpected social media reset has inevitably drawn fresh attention to his ongoing contract situation.Supporters noticed on Wednesday that Vinicius' Instagram account, followed by more than 64 million people, had been completely wiped.Every post disappeared from his profile, while his biography, profile photograph and story highlights were also removed. Although footballers occasionally clear their social media accounts before new campaigns or commercial launches, Vinicius has offered no explanation for the decision.The timing has inevitably fuelled fresh discussion because it comes while negotiations over his future remain unresolved.Real Madrid are understood to have offered the 26-year-old a new contract worth around $25.5 million per season, but no agreement has yet been announced.With his current deal entering its final year, discussions over a long-term extension remain ongoing.The social media activity stands in contrast to events on the training ground.Vinicius only returned to Real Madrid's training base earlier this week after his post-World Cup break and has now joined José Mourinho's squad as preparations continue for the 2026-27 season.Speaking toafter returning, the Brazilian gave little indication that his future was in doubt."It has gone very well, getting to know the new coach and the new players, and training very hard."He also revealed Mourinho's message to him."Mourinho wants me to be as I have always been: happy, cheerful and playing my style of football."Talks involving Vinicius' representatives, Real Madrid general director José Ángel Sánchez and chief scout Juni Calafat also took place in Madrid on Wednesday, with reports suggesting the club remain optimistic about reaching an agreement.Despite those positive signs, Vinicius has remained one of the most discussed names of the summer transfer window.Arsenal have repeatedly been linked with the Brazilian, although neither club has publicly confirmed negotiations. When Mikel Arteta was asked about the forward during Arsenal's pre-season tour last week, he smiled before saying only that the Premier League champions remained "very active" in the market and expected further movement before the window closed.Around the same time, Vinicius' representatives at Roc Nation Sports International issued a strongly worded statement condemning what they described as "fake and damaging information" published about their clients.Without mentioning Vinicius specifically, the agency said it could not "stand idle when unprofessional and uninformed media publish fake and damaging information for attention-seeking purposes," adding that such reporting was "disruptive, harmful and libellous" and urging media outlets to be more accountable.The statement arrived amid widespread transfer speculation involving several Roc Nation clients, including Vinicius.For now, there is nothing to indicate that Vinicius' social media clear-out is directly connected to his contract negotiations.Real Madrid are still believed to be confident of keeping one of their most important players, while Mourinho has made clear that the Brazilian remains central to his plans for the new season.Until an agreement is signed, however, every development surrounding Vinicius is likely to attract heightened attention. Wednesday's Instagram reset may ultimately prove to be nothing more than a personal decision, but with negotiations continuing and interest from elsewhere refusing to disappear, it has inevitably become another talking point in one of football's most closely watched contract sagas.
Article Summary: Vinicius Jr deletes everything from Instagram as Real Madrid future remains under the spotlight. Brazilian returned to pre-season training under José Mourinho earlier this week. Real Madrid are understood to have offered the 26-year-old a new contract worth around $25.5 million per season, but no agreement has yet been announced.

Article Title: Why Mohamed Salah chose a Turkish club nobody expected over Saudi Arabia or MLS
Article Text:
Egypt's Mohamed Salah wearing his new Trabzonspor team jersey gestures to supporters as he arrives at the airport in Istanbul, Turkey, Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Samet Yalcin/DIA Photo via AP)

A move shaped by football as much as finances

Why Trabzonspor made sense

There is still a football case to be made

Argentina's Lionel Messi controls the ball under the watch of Egypt's Mohamed Salah, left, during the World Cup round of 16 soccer match between Argentina and Egypt in Atlanta, Tuesday, July 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Colin Hubbard)

The transfer reflects a changing Turkish league

"I think Liverpool fans, and people who love watching Salah, will definitely take notice and start following the league,"

"When I moved there, my family and friends started watching games because they didn't really know much about Turkish football before. Salah's move will make people sit up and watch more of the league."

"The league is getting stronger every year and you're seeing more and more big names joining. Salah is probably the biggest name to move to Turkey in recent years. It shows the league is growing and it might persuade other top players to consider going there. There are great stadiums, great cities and it's a competitive league."

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

"I loved it. Everyone helps you settle in and the people are really friendly.

When foreign players arrive, the clubs do everything they can to help them."

When Mohamed Salah 's Liverpool career came to an end, there was little doubt his next move would place him alongside football's biggest names. Saudi Arabia offered the prospect of sharing a league with Cristiano Ronaldo, while Major League Soccer could have set up regular meetings with Lionel Messi. Even within Europe, there were expectations that one of Turkey's traditional Istanbul giants would eventually secure his signature. Trabzonspor, by comparison, barely featured in those conversations.That changed on Thursday when the Egyptian agreed a two-year contract with the club, bringing one of the most decorated Premier League careers of the modern era to an unexpected but carefully considered next chapter.It would be difficult to argue that money played no part in Salah's decision. Few transfers involving players of his stature ever do. Trabzonspor have committed significant resources to complete the deal, confirming in a filing to the Turkish stock exchange that Salah will earn around $19.5 million per season and receive 20% of the revenue generated from merchandise bearing his name.Yet the figures alone do not explain why he chose Turkey.Saudi clubs had the financial strength to offer considerably more, while MLS presented another attractive alternative for a player whose commercial appeal extends well beyond football. Remaining in Europe, however, appears to have carried greater importance than pursuing the largest possible contract.Trabzonspor finished third in last season's Super Lig and will enter the UEFA Europa League play-offs later this month. Victory would take them into the league phase, while defeat would still guarantee UEFA Conference League football. Although the Turkish top flight is not regarded among Europe's elite—Opta currently ranks it as the 14th strongest domestic league in world football, behind competitions such as Denmark's Superliga, Poland's Ekstraklasa and even England's Championship, it still offers Salah regular European competition in one of the continent's most demanding football environments.For a player who helped Egypt reach the knockout stages of this summer's FIFA World Cup, continuing to compete in Europe appears to have been an important part of the calculation.If Salah's priority was to remain in Europe, Trabzonspor was still not the destination many expected.For decades, Galatasaray, Fenerbahçe and Beşiktaş have dominated Turkish football's biggest transfer stories. Salah himself was linked with several of those clubs during recent windows, and reports suggested Beşiktaş came close before negotiations over the financial structure of the deal broke down.Trabzonspor, however, offered something equally valuable: importance.The club may not possess the global profile of their Istanbul rivals, but they remain one of Turkey's most successful sides, having won seven league titles, lifted the Super Lig as recently as 2021-22 and added last season's Turkish Cup. They are also entering a season with realistic ambitions of returning to European group-stage football.For Salah, there is another attraction that is perhaps less obvious.Rather than arriving as another established star in a squad already full of headline names, he becomes the central figure around whom the club's sporting and commercial ambitions can be built. That was evident before he had even reached Trabzon, with hundreds of supporters gathering to welcome the biggest signing in the club's history.Age inevitably shapes the conversation whenever an elite player changes clubs in his mid-thirties, but Salah's recent performances suggest there is still considerably more to offer than reputation alone.His final season at Liverpool was complicated by a deteriorating relationship with head coach Arne Slot, eventually leading both parties to agree to terminate the final year of his contract. Even so, Salah finished with 12 goals in all competitions.Only a year earlier he had produced arguably one of the finest individual campaigns of his career, scoring 34 goals and providing 23 assists as Liverpool won the Premier League. He then carried that form into the 2026 FIFA World Cup, helping Egypt reach the knockout stages with one goal and two assists in five appearances.Fatih Tekke is therefore not signing a player whose value rests solely on past achievements. Trabzonspor are expected to deploy Salah in the familiar right-sided attacking role that defined his years at Liverpool, allowing him to cut inside onto his stronger left foot while remaining the focal point of the team's attackSalah's arrival also says something about the direction of Turkish football.The Super Lig has steadily become a destination for established international players who still believe they have more to contribute at the highest level. Victor Osimhen, Leroy Sané, İlkay Gündoğan, Nathan Aké and Leandro Trossard are among the prominent names now playing in Turkey, while Trabzonspor already count André Onana, Ruslan Malinovskyi and Stefan Savić among their squad.Former Rangers midfielder Ryan Jack, who spent the past two seasons in Turkey, believes Salah's arrival will bring even greater international attention to the competition.Jack told BBC Sport.Jack believes the transfer also reflects the league's growing reputation.His own experience left a similarly positive impression.Salah could have chosen a league where the commercial rewards were greater or one where the global spotlight was brighter. Instead, he has chosen a club that offers European football, an ambitious sporting project and the opportunity to remain at the centre of it.That may not have been the outcome most expected when he left Liverpool, but viewed through those priorities, Trabzonspor becomes a far less surprising destination than it first appeared.
Article Summary: Mohamed Salah has signed for Turkish club Trabzonspor on a two-year deal. The Egyptian striker will earn around $19.5 million per season. The move reflects a changing Turkish league as well as a move shaped by football as much as finances.

South Korean police have raided the Korea Football Association (KFA) as part of an ongoing investigation into alleged irregularities surrounding the appointment of former men's national team head coach Hong Myung-bo in 2024. The search comes little over a month after Hong resigned following South Korea's disappointing group-stage exit at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with investigators seeking documents linked to the federation's coaching appointment process.Police carried out search and seizure operations on Thursday at the KFA headquarters in Cheonan, around 90 kilometres south of Seoul, as well as the KFA House in central Seoul.According to Yonhap, the raids are part of an investigation into allegations that the federation unfairly intervened in Hong's appointment as national team head coach in July 2024.Investigators are seeking documents to determine whether senior KFA officials, including former federation president Chung Mong-kyu and former technical director Lee Lim-saeng, improperly influenced the appointment process.The investigation began around two years ago but has attracted renewed scrutiny following South Korea's disappointing World Cup campaign.Hong's appointment was controversial from the outset, with critics alleging that the federation failed to follow its established hiring procedures.According to the allegations, Lee Lim-saeng, despite having no authority over coaching appointments, personally offered Hong the national team job during a meeting at a bakery near the former coach's home.A civic group later filed a criminal complaint against Hong and Chung, alleging obstruction of duties, breach of trust, coercion and intimidation in relation to the appointment.Police questioned Hong as a suspect on Tuesday as the investigation gathered pace.Expectations had been high before the tournament, with South Korean media describing the squad as a "golden generation" led by captain Son Heung-min alongside Bayern Munich defender Kim Min-jae and former Paris Saint-Germain midfielder Lee Kang-in.Instead, South Korea were eliminated in the group stage, prompting widespread criticism of both the team's performances and the federation's leadership.Hong's decision to leave Son on the bench during the first half of the decisive World Cup match against South Africa particularly baffled supporters and became one of the most heavily criticised tactical calls of the campaign.When the team returned home in June, Hong was greeted by boos and chants of "Hong out!" at the airport, while fans applauded the players walking behind him. Afterwards, Hong admitted he was struggling to understand what had gone wrong.President Lee Jae Myung also weighed in on the team's early exit, blaming the failure on "incompetent people" being promoted into leadership positions and referring to "loyalty and factionalism" influencing recruitment at the highest level of South Korean football.The KFA declined to comment when contacted by AFP.At a parliamentary hearing held in late July, lawmakers questioned Hong and former KFA president Chung Mong-kyu over the federation's management and the circumstances surrounding the coaching appointment.During the hearing, Hong said he took "full responsibility" for South Korea's disappointing World Cup campaign.Lawmakers also questioned reports claiming Hong earned an annual salary of 3.8 billion won (approximately). Hong insisted the reported figure was inaccurate but declined to disclose the actual amount.The police investigation into Hong's appointment remains ongoing as authorities continue examining documents seized during Thursday's raids.
